introduction: This fourth Sunday of Lent is Laetare Sunday, and rose vestments may be worn. Samuel anoints David, for the Lord looks not at appearances but at the heart. In the Gospel, Jesus heals a man born blind, who comes to see more and more clearly who Jesus is, while others become blind. Paul urges us to live as children of light. Where catechumens celebrate the second scrutiny, we pray for them.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord is our shepherd and our light. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may live as a child of light and help others to see. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the catechumens: that Christ may open their eyes and lead them to the light of faith. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the blind and those who live with disabilities: that they may be respected and helped. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are blind to their own sins or to the needs of others: that Christ may heal their sight. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may say with the man born blind, Lord, I believe. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you look at the heart and your Son is the light of the world. Open our eyes to see him, and help us to walk as children of light. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: I was blind, now I see
reflection.body:
God sends Samuel to anoint a new king from among Jesse's sons. Samuel sees the eldest, tall and impressive, and thinks he must be the one. But God says, "Don't look on his face, or on the height of his stature... For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart." Seven sons pass by, and none is chosen. The youngest, David, is out with the sheep. He is the one God has chosen.

The Gospel is a long story about seeing and not seeing. Jesus sees a man blind from birth. His disciples ask whose sin caused the blindness. Jesus says it is no one's: "that the works of God might be revealed in him." And he adds, "I am the light of the world." He makes mud, puts it on the man's eyes, and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam. The man comes back seeing.

What follows is a series of interrogations. The neighbors argue about whether it is really him. The Pharisees question him, then his parents, then him again. The man's answers grow stronger. First he calls Jesus "A man called Jesus," then "a prophet," and finally he stands up to the authorities: "One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see." They throw him out.

Then Jesus finds him and asks, "Do you believe in the Son of God?" The man answers, "Lord, I believe!" and worships him. The man who was blind now sees fully. The ones who claim to see have become blind.

Paul tells us, "you were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light."

Today we pray for the catechumens, who are being brought from darkness to light. This week, ask Jesus to heal your own blindness: to God's presence, to your sins, to the people around you. And give thanks for the gift of faith.
